title: How Leaders Can Elevate Dignity in the Workplace
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article treats dignity as innate rather than earned, distinguishing it from respect and trust, and argues leaders can honor or unintentionally undermine it through everyday actions. It flags specific dignity risks: policies that reduce people to numbers or labels, group emails that implicitly target some people, and environments that discourage disagreement. The piece frames the right to disagree as a core component of workplace dignity, not a separate issue. It closes by describing the kind of relationship — safe, heard, validated — that leaders should aim to create for every team member.
points: Dignity is innate, unlike respect and trust, which are earned through actions over time.
Policies that assign numbers, rankings, or labels can unintentionally strip away people's dignity.
Group emails or messages that implicitly target some people damage dignity even when unintended.
The ability to disagree openly without dismissal is framed as core to workplace dignity.
Leaders are urged to give people space to express themselves authentically and without judgment.
quotes: Leaders don’t give people dignity. They honor it through their actions and treatment of others. Or fail to.
In other words, it is easy to do harm to dignity without knowing it.
Any action or policy that lumps people together and takes away their individuality has the potential to diminish the dignity of team members.
Dignity in the workplace is also dependent on the ability to disagree.
Good leaders are conscious of this and create relationships where others feel safe, heard, validated, recognized, and valued.
